lesson.title: How Long Until It Happens? Geometric Probability in Action
lesson.summary: Applying the geometric formula answers precise questions about exactly when a first success is likely to land, while a short complement argument answers how long you might have to wait for it.
lesson.body:
With the geometric distribution's formula in hand, P(X = k) = (1 minus p)^(k minus 1) x p, you can answer exact questions about when a first success is likely to land, the same way the binomial formula answered exact questions about how many successes occur.

Suppose a carnival game pays out a prize on 20% of spins, independent from spin to spin, so p = 0.2. What is the probability that a player's first win happens on exactly the 4th spin? Using the formula with k = 4: P(X = 4) = (1 minus 0.2)^3 x 0.2 = (0.8)^3 x 0.2. Computing (0.8)^3 = 0.8 x 0.8 x 0.8 = 0.512, then multiplying by 0.2 gives 0.512 x 0.2 = 0.1024. There is about a 10.24% chance the player's first win comes on that exact 4th spin, no earlier and no later.

A related but different question: what is the probability it takes more than 3 spins to win at all? This does not require the geometric formula directly. It just requires the first 3 spins to all fail, since more than 3 spins means no success yet through spin 3. By independence, that probability is simply (1 minus p) multiplied by itself 3 times: (0.8)^3 = 0.512. So there is a 51.2% chance the player is still waiting for a first win after 3 spins, meaning more than half the time, 3 spins is not enough.

Notice these two answers are related but answer different questions: 0.1024 is the chance the win lands on exactly spin 4, while 0.512 is the chance the win still has not happened through spin 3 (which necessarily includes the possibility of it landing on spin 4, 5, 6, or any later spin). Both calculations lean on the same independence assumption from the geometric setting: each spin's outcome has no bearing on any other spin's outcome, so probabilities of strings of failures multiply cleanly.
